stranding.title: Found a stranded
stranding.intro: Stay calm, keep your distance and call for help. Trained responders know what to do — a quick call is the most useful thing you can do.
stranding.callText: If the animal is alive, or you’re not sure who to contact, call the stranding hotline. Trained responders will tell you what to do next.
do: Keep a safe distance, and keep people and dogs away.
Note the exact location, the time, and the animal’s size and condition.
Take photos from a distance, if it’s safe to do so.
Stay nearby until help arrives, if you can.
dont: Don’t push or drag it back into the sea — it’s probably sick or exhausted and will often strand again.
Don’t touch it: marine mammals can pass diseases to people and pets.
Don’t pull on its flippers or tail, or cover its blowhole.
Don’t take bones, teeth or other parts — these are protected species.
stranding.deadText: Report it anyway. Dead animals tell scientists a great deal about the health, diet and threats facing the population.
stranding.networksIntro: Trained teams who respond to strandings and study the animals they find.

stranding.ctaText: Add a report on WhaleTale too, so the record isn’t lost.

about.title: A field guide
about.intro: WhaleTale brings together the science of the whales, dolphins, porpoises and seals of Portuguese waters — from the mainland coast to the Azores and Madeira — and invites everyone to help study them.

mission.title: Learn
mission.text: Peer-reviewed science in plain language, in Portuguese, English and French.

mission.title: Observe
mission.text: Species profiles and field tips to help you recognise what you see, and where and when to look.

mission.title: Contribute
mission.text: Sightings and stranding reports that add to what we know about these animals.

about.methodologyIntro: Trust is everything for a science resource. These are the rules we hold ourselves to.
methodology: Facts come from peer-reviewed research and standard references, such as the IUCN Red List and the Portuguese Red Book of Mammals.
Where studies disagree, we give ranges or rounded values rather than a single, falsely precise figure.
Every page lists the sources behind it.
Field reports are checked before they join the record.
Spotted a mistake? Tell us and we’ll correct it.
about.partnersIntro: WhaleTale is independent. Partners help us grow, but never decide what we say.
policy: Partners and sponsors have no say over scientific content.
Sponsored features are always clearly labelled.
No sponsorship ever appears in the stranding or reporting pages, or inside the science content.
We don’t accept support from organisations whose activities conflict with the protection of marine mammals.
about.partnersEmpty: We’re looking for our first partners: research groups, NGOs and foundations that share our mission.
about.contactText: Spotted an error, know a resource we missed, or want to work with us? We’d love to hear from you.

where.title: Where and when
where.intro: Portugal’s waters stretch from the mainland coast to two Atlantic archipelagos. Each has its own residents, visitors and seasons.

mainland.title: Mainland coast
mainland.teaser: From the Sado estuary to the headlands of the Algarve, a long Atlantic coast shaped by upwelling.
mainland.intro: Mainland Portugal faces the Atlantic for more than 900 km. Seasonal upwelling makes its shelf waters rich in sardine and other small fish, which draw common dolphins in large numbers. The Sado estuary is home to a small resident community of bottlenose dolphins, and harbour porpoises are found mostly in the north and centre.

azores.title: Azores
azores.teaser: Nine volcanic islands in the middle of the North Atlantic, where deep water lies close to shore.
azores.intro: The Azores sit on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, with depths of more than 1,000 m a few kilometres from the coast. Sperm whales are present all year, and in spring blue, fin and sei whales pass through on their way north. More than 20 cetacean species have been recorded here, making the archipelago one of Europe’s best places to watch whales.

madeira.title: Madeira
madeira.teaser: A subtropical archipelago with deep, warm water and one of the last monk seal colonies.
madeira.intro: Madeira’s steep volcanic slopes drop quickly into deep, warm water. Bryde’s whales, Atlantic spotted dolphins and short-finned pilot whales are regulars, and the Desertas Islands shelter one of the last colonies of the Mediterranean monk seal.

where.watchingIntro: A good encounter is one where the animals carry on as if you weren’t there.
watching: Keep your distance and let the animals decide how close to come.
Approach slowly from the side and slightly behind — never head-on, and never cut through a group.
Keep a steady, slow speed near animals and avoid sudden changes of course.
Limit your time with each group, and leave if they show signs of disturbance.
Never feed, touch or swim with wild cetaceans or seals.
Choose licensed operators that follow the national and regional whale-watching rules.

privacy.title: Your data
privacy.intro: What we collect when you send a report or sign up for updates, and what we do with it.

sections.title: What we collect
text: When you send a report: what you saw, where and when, any photos, your name if you choose to give it, and your account’s email address.
When you create an account: your name, email address and sign-in details.
When you sign up for updates: your email address and the language you use the site in.

sections.title: Why we collect it
text: Reports are used to study and protect marine mammals. We use your email only to ask about your report, or to send the updates you signed up for.

sections.title: What is published
text: Verified reports appear on the site with the species, place, date and your name, if you gave it. Your email address is never published.
Verified records may be shared with researchers and open biodiversity databases such as GBIF, without your email address.

sections.title: Where it is stored
text: Accounts are managed by Clerk, our sign-in provider. Reports and sign-ups are stored with Sanity, the service that runs our content. Only the WhaleTale team can see personal details.

sections.title: Your rights
text: You can ask to see, correct or delete your personal data at any time, and unsubscribe from updates whenever you like. You can also complain to the Portuguese data protection authority (CNPD).

privacy.cookiesText: We only use the cookies the site needs to work: to remember your language and to keep you signed in. There are no advertising or analytics cookies.

cookies.title: Cookie policy
cookies.summary: We only use essential cookies. No advertising, analytics or tracking.
cookies.intro: Cookies are small files a website saves in your browser. Ours are all needed for the site to work, so no consent is required and there’s nothing to switch off.
cookies.essentialText: These remember your language and keep you signed in.

list.name: __cf_bm, _cfuvid
list.purpose: Protect our sign-in service from bots and abuse.

sections.title: Other services
text: The map loads tiles from OpenStreetMap, which sees your IP address but sets no cookies. Google and other sign-in options may set their own cookies on their own sites.

sections.title: Managing cookies
text: You can delete or block cookies in your browser settings, but you won’t be able to sign in or send reports. If we ever add optional cookies, we’ll ask first.

help.title: How you can help
help.intro: Practical things anyone can do about the threats this species faces.

fishing.title: Fish responsibly
fishing.text: Never leave lines or nets behind, and report lost gear. If you see an animal tangled in rope or net, don’t try to free it yourself — call the stranding hotline so a trained team can help.

noise.title: Keep it quiet
noise.text: Near cetaceans, slow down, keep a steady course and avoid sudden changes of speed. Less engine noise means less stress for animals that live by sound.

boats.title: Give them space
boats.text: Keep your distance, never chase or cut off a group, and let animals choose to approach. Choose whale-watching operators that follow the rules.

plastic.title: Cut the plastic
plastic.text: Avoid single-use plastics, take your rubbish home from the beach and join a local clean-up. Plastic and chemical pollution end up in the food chain.

climate.title: Choose sustainable seafood
climate.text: Pick certified seafood from healthy stocks and cut your carbon footprint: well-managed fisheries and a stable climate keep prey available.

strandings.title: Report every stranding
strandings.text: Dead and stranded animals tell scientists how populations are doing. A quick report helps track disease and other threats.

report.title: Share your sightings
report.text: Every record helps researchers follow this species along our coast and around the islands.
